Apes
āps
n. pl. (exotic animals brought home by the fleets of Solomon; a mark of imperial luxury)
Old English apa. The Hebrew qoph is a loanword travelling with the animal itself along the trade routes to Tarshish, appearing in Scripture only in the two parallel accounts of Solomon's navy.

Biblical Definition

Apes appear in the Bible exactly twice, both times in an inventory. “For the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram: once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks” (1Ki 10:22), and Chronicles repeats it of Huram's ships (2Ch 9:21). They are the tail end of a list that begins with bullion and ends with curiosities — a king so rich that novelty had become a category of import. The whole chapter runs to excess, and the chapter after it in Kings records what the wealth and the wives together did to Solomon's heart.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an ape as a genus of quadrumanous animals without a tail, and figuratively one who imitates another servilely.

expand to see more

APE, n. A genus of quadrumanous animals, the character of which is, that they have no tails. In common use, the word extends to monkeys of all sorts.

APE, n. One who imitates servilely, in allusion to the manners of the ape; a silly fellow.

APE, v.t. To imitate servilely; to mimick, as an ape imitates human actions.

Key Scripture

1Ki 10:22 — "For the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram: once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks."

2Ch 9:21 — "For the king's ships went to Tarshish with the servants of Huram: every three years once came the ships of Tarshish bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks."

Job 9:10 — "Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number."

Isa 40:26 — "Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth."

Modern Corruption

Solomon's apes are a footnote to a reign that gained the world and lost its heart, and Deuteronomy had forbidden the multiplying beforehand.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 17 legislated for a king before Israel had one: he shall not multiply horses to himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt to multiply horses; neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away; neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold. First Kings 10 and 11 read like a deliberate audit against that statute. Horses out of Egypt, silver as stones in Jerusalem, seven hundred wives, and three-year voyages bringing apes and peacocks — and then the sentence: his wives turned away his heart. The apes are not the sin; they are the receipt.

The corruption to name is the assumption that prosperity vindicates. Solomon's reign is the strongest case in Scripture for the opposite reading — that God may grant a man everything he asked and everything he did not, and the man may still end his life building high places for Chemosh and Molech. The prosperity teaching that reads wealth as evidence of divine approval has to skip 1 Kings 11 entirely to survive, and so does its secular cousin, which reads success as evidence of virtue. Scripture files the apes under warning.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qoph (H6971), ape; Tarshish (H8659), the far trading port; oni (H590), a fleet of ships.

expand to see more

Hebrew qoph (H6971) — ape; 1 Kings 10:22, 2 Chronicles 9:21 only.

Hebrew Tarshish (H8659) — Tarshish, a distant port; 1 Kings 10:22, Jonah 1:3, Isaiah 23:1.

Hebrew oni (H590) — ships, a fleet; 1 Kings 10:22, Isaiah 33:21.

Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to multiply, increase; Deuteronomy 17:16, 17:17.

Hebrew natah (H5186) — to turn aside, incline; 1 Kings 11:3, 11:4.

Usage

"“Bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks” — the fleet's three-year manifest."

"“Every three years once came the ships of Tarshish” — Chronicles' parallel record."

"An inventory of curiosities from a reign that ended in high places."
